title: Lively v. Wild Oats Markets, Inc.
lead: A diverse local defendant removes a California injury action, the plaintiff remains silent, and a judge later tries to remand on the forum-defendant ground.

actors.name: Emma C. Lively
actors.role: New York plaintiff alleging a California store slip and fall.

actors.name: Wild Oats Markets
actors.role: Diverse store defendant whose California citizenship was uncontested on appeal.

actors.name: Federal District Court
actors.role: Court ordering remand on its own eight months after removal.

proceedings: Wild Oats removed; Lively made no timely remand motion.
The District Court remanded sua sponte after questioning the defendant’s principal place of business.
The Ninth Circuit reviewed the unauthorized remand, vacated it, and returned the case for further proceedings.
limits: The decision did not decide negligence, actual principal-place-of-business facts, snap removal, or today’s circuit alignment. Its formal disposition was vacatur and remand, not the textbook’s shorthand reversal.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with complete effective canonical brief; no new independent full-opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A California store accident produces a removed diversity suit
sections.cue: What citizenship facts were disputed initially?
paragraphs: Emma C. Lively alleged that she slipped and fell at a California Wild Oats store. She filed a state personal-injury action on September 26, 2003. Wild Oats removed January 8, 2004, asserting Delaware incorporation, a Colorado principal place of business, New York plaintiff citizenship, and more than $75,000 at stake. Lively did not object.

About eight months later, after discovery and a defense summary-judgment motion, the District Court questioned whether Wild Oats was actually principally based in California. Wild Oats answered that even California citizenship preserved diversity with a New Yorker. It would trigger the forum-defendant restriction on removal, but Lively’s thirty-day objection period had expired.

The judge treated that restriction as jurisdictional and remanded under § 1447(c). Wild Oats did not contest California citizenship on appeal. The appellate question was the consequence of local-defendant removal in an otherwise diverse case, not resolution of its headquarters or the accident.

sections.title: The Ninth Circuit separates original jurisdiction from removal eligibility
sections.cue: Why could this citizenship defect be waived?
paragraphs: The then-§ 1441(b) barred diversity removal by a properly joined and served forum citizen. That restriction differed from § 1332’s original diversity requirements. A California defendant and New York plaintiff could remain diverse despite improper California removal.

Paez’s panel used procedural and nonjurisdictional interchangeably for this classification, while acknowledging that citizenship was more substantive than ordinary filing mechanics. The statute’s restriction remained enforceable on a timely motion. Spencer, involving a local party added only after removal, had not previously resolved this question because no initial violation existed there.

The panel traced § 1447(c) from improvident removal without jurisdiction, through the 1988 deadline for defects in removal procedure, to the 1996 deadline for every defect other than subject-matter jurisdiction. The change addressed restrictions that did not fit narrow procedural mechanics but left original jurisdiction intact.

sources.pinpoint: Jurisdiction and restriction; Statutory history; court PDF 3–4 & nn.2–4,9–11 & n.8

sections.title: The appellate-review bar does not protect every order citing § 1447(c)
sections.cue: How could the panel examine remand power?
paragraphs: Lively argued § 1447(d) barred review because the District Court labeled its order jurisdictional. Under Thermtron and later cases, subsections (c) and (d) operated together: the bar protected remands within statutory authority, not every order invoking the section.

Nonjurisdictional defects required a motion within thirty days. Actual subject-matter absence required remand whenever discovered before final judgment. Classification therefore determined both district-court authority and appellate review. The panel could determine its own jurisdiction and the intertwined issue; § 1291 supplied affirmative jurisdiction because remand ended the federal proceeding despite no injury judgment. This did not authorize appeals from every allegedly erroneous jurisdictional remand.

sections.title: Policy and precedent support the thirty-day limit
sections.cue: Why was there no special pretrial exception?
paragraphs: Diversity removal guards against local prejudice to outsiders. A local defendant ordinarily needs no such protection, so the forum-defendant rule lets plaintiffs choose prompt return or accept federal court by silence. Mandatory sua sponte remand after waiver could defeat both parties’ preference and the plaintiff’s choice.

Eight of nine other circuits then addressing the issue agreed on nonjurisdictionality; the panel rejected the Eighth Circuit’s Hurt approach. That was the reported 2006 alignment, not a current survey. Not every removal restriction destroyed original jurisdiction.

The District Court had read Grubbs as curing the problem only after a merits judgment. The panel read it as distinguishing a defective route into federal court from original judicial power. Its own cases applied that reasoning to summary judgment too. A waivable defect did not remain jurisdictional until trial, and distinguishing complete silence from late objection did not repair Hurt’s premise: true jurisdictional absence demanded attention either way.

sources.pinpoint: Policy; Other circuits and Grubbs; court PDF 11–15 & nn.9–13

sections.title: The order is vacated and the injury claim continues below
sections.cue: What did the appellate decision resolve?
paragraphs: Lively had not timely invoked the restriction. The District Court therefore exceeded § 1447(c) by remanding on its own, allowing appellate review of that unauthorized order. On July 27, 2006, the unanimous panel of Paez, Hawkins, and visiting District Judge Wake vacated and remanded for further proceedings.
The ruling preserved the distinction between diversity jurisdiction and a waivable removal defect. It decided no negligence or damages issue, and no separate opinions were filed.
